types.name: Send stream records
types.desc: dmu_replay_record_t headers and their payloads: BEGIN, OBJECT, FREEOBJECTS, OBJECT_RANGE, WRITE, WRITE_EMBEDDED, SPILL, FREE, REDACT, END.

types.name: DMU buffer
types.desc: dmu_buf_impl_t: one logical block of one object, held in memory (plus its dirty records).

types.name: ARC buffer
types.desc: arc_buf_t / arc_buf_hdr_t: cached block, keyed by DVA + birth txg.

types.name: Physical payload
types.desc: abd_t: the bytes exactly as they sit on disk (compressed / encrypted / padded to ashift).

types.name: I/O request
types.desc: zio_t moving through the pipeline (logical zio or a vdev child zio).

types.name: Block pointer
types.desc: blkptr_t: DVAs + sizes + checksum + birth txg; here also send_range entries, which carry a copy of the block pointer.

types.name: Transaction
types.desc: dmu_tx_t membership / a txg number being opened, quiesced or synced.

types.name: Control
types.desc: Calls that carry no payload: locks, wakeups, throttling, accounting, callbacks. Draw dashed.

contexts.name: Open context: the calling thread, inside a dmu_tx
Kernel, in the thread of the calling process (an ioctl on /dev/zfs, mount(2) or umount(2)) or a helper thread it starts, outside syncing context and outside any dmu_tx
Syncing context: txg_sync thread or dp_sync_taskq workers, one txg at a time
A dedicated kernel thread or zthr
Runs in whichever context calls it

groups.title: Sender userspace (zfs send)
groups.summary: The zfs command, libzfs and libzfs_core: option parsing, resume tokens, replication packages.

groups.title: Send entry (ioctl, dmu_send)
groups.summary: The ioctl, the choice of from point and the BEGIN record.

groups.title: Send thread pipeline
groups.summary: Traversal, merge and reader threads, then the main thread turning ranges into records.

groups.title: Block reads (shared with the I/O graph)
groups.summary: Where the sender's reads go: the ARC if the block is cached, otherwise a direct zio.

groups.title: Stream and resume token
groups.summary: The bytes between the two machines, and the token that restarts an interrupted transfer.

groups.title: Receiver userspace (zfs receive)
groups.summary: Reads the BEGIN record, checks the destination, hands the file descriptor to the kernel.

groups.title: Receive entry, begin and end
groups.summary: The ioctl and the sync tasks that create the receiving dataset and later switch it into place.

groups.title: Receive threads and record handlers
groups.summary: The reader in the ioctl thread, the writer thread and one handler per record type.

groups.title: DMU and txg (shared with the I/O graph)
groups.summary: Transactions, dirty records and the txg sync that finally writes the received data.

nodes.title: Administrator
nodes.role: The person or script typing the command. Every path in this graph that a command starts begins with a wire from this node; the arrows that come back into a command node are its results, errors and refusals.

nodes.title: zfs send (cmd/zfs)
nodes.role: Parses the send options: -i / -I name the incremental source (a snapshot with @ or a bookmark with #), -R asks for a replication stream, -c compressed, -w raw (which also sets -c, -e and -L), -L large blocks, -e embedded blocks, -t a resume token. Without -R or -I the send goes through zfs_send_one(); -R and -I go through zfs_send(); -t goes to zfs_send_resume(). -D is accepted but only prints that deduplicated streams are no longer supported.

nodes.title: libzfs: zfs_send_one() / zfs_send_resume()

ref.code: zfs_send_one(zfs_handle_t *zhp, const char *from, int fd, sendflags_t *flags,

nodes.role: Turns the command flags into lzc_send_flags, runs the optional size estimate and progress thread, then calls libzfs_core. For -t it decodes the token (hex, checked with fletcher-4, zlib-uncompressed into an nvlist), finds the snapshot by the token's toguid, and takes the resume object, offset and the -L / -c / -e / -w flags from the token.

nodes.title: libzfs: replication stream (-R, -I)
nodes.role: Builds a compound stream in userspace: a BEGIN record marked DMU_COMPOUNDSTREAM (with -R its payload lists every filesystem, snapshot and property) closed by its own END, then one ordinary substream per snapshot, each requested from the kernel with the legacy ZFS_IOC_SEND and incremental from the previous snapshot, then a final END. The kernel only ever produces single-snapshot streams.

nodes.title: libzfs_core: lzc_send_resume_redacted()

ref.code: lzc_send_resume_redacted(const char *snapname, const char *from, int fd,
lzc_send_redacted(const char *snapname, const char *from, int fd,
lzc_send_resume_redacted_cb_impl(const char *snapname, const char *from, int fd,

nodes.role: Packs the arguments into an nvlist (fd, fromsnap, largeblockok, embedok, compressok, rawok, savedok, resume_object, resume_offset, redactbook) and issues ZFS_IOC_SEND_NEW. On Linux, lzc_send_wrapper() puts a pipe and a copying thread in front of an output that is not already a pipe.

nodes.title: Send ioctl
nodes.role: Kernel entry. Sets the stream output function to dump_bytes(), which writes every header and payload to the caller's file descriptor with zfs_file_write() (through a one-thread z_send taskq where kernel stacks are small), then calls dmu_send(). The legacy zfs_ioc_send(), still used by replication streams, calls dmu_send_obj() with dataset object numbers instead of names.

nodes.title: dmu_send() / dmu_send_obj()

ref.code: dmu_send(const char *tosnap, const char *fromsnap, boolean_t embedok,
dmu_send_obj(const char *pool, uint64_t tosnap, uint64_t fromsnap,

nodes.role: Holds the pool and the snapshot to send (owning the dataset instead when a filesystem itself is sent). A non-raw send holds it with DS_HOLD_FLAG_DECRYPT, so an encrypted dataset needs its key loaded; a raw send does not. Resolves the incremental source, marks the stream as a clone stream when the source is in another filesystem, then calls dmu_send_impl().

nodes.title: Incremental source: snapshot or bookmark
nodes.role: Reduces the from point to a zfs_bookmark_phys_t: creation txg, guid and IV set guid. A snapshot must be an earlier snapshot of the same lineage (dsl_dataset_is_before(), otherwise EXDEV); a bookmark is checked the same way by dsl_bookmark_lookup(). Nothing else about the from point is used, so a bookmark, which keeps no blocks, is as good a source as the snapshot it was made from.

nodes.title: dmu_send_impl(): BEGIN, threads, END
nodes.role: Chooses the stream's feature flags from the request and from what the dataset uses (LARGE_BLOCKS with -L or -w if large blocks are active, EMBED_DATA with -e unless the dataset is encrypted, COMPRESSED with -c or -w, RAW with -w on an encrypted dataset, LZ4, ZSTD, LARGE_DNODE, RESUMING, REDACTED). Writes BEGIN with an optional nvlist payload, starts the worker threads, then runs the main loop: take a range from the reader queue, do_dump() it, stop on a signal. Ends with END, or with no END at all for a saved send.

nodes.title: to_ds traversal thread
nodes.role: Walks the snapshot being sent with traverse_dataset_resume() and turns every block pointer it is handed into a send_range: OBJECT for a dnode (with a copy of the dnode), OBJECT_RANGE for a meta-dnode data block, DATA for a level-0 block (with a copy of its block pointer), HOLE for a hole, REDACT for a redacted block. Queues them in order and finishes with an end-of-stream marker. The queues between the worker threads are limited in bytes.

nodes.title: traverse_visitbp(): birth-txg pruning
nodes.role: Pre-order walk of the block tree. A block pointer whose birth txg is at or before fromtxg is skipped together with everything below it: copy-on-write rewrites every indirect block above a changed block in the same txg, so an old parent proves the whole subtree is unchanged. A raw send of an encrypted dataset compares the physical birth (zfs rewrite -P keeps the logical one); other sends compare the logical birth. Holes carry a birth txg too, so deleted data is found the same way; holes with birth 0 (written before the hole_birth feature) are always visited while send_holes_without_birth_time is 1, its default. Indirect blocks are read through the ARC, with read-ahead of the next few. On a resumed send, resume_skip_check() skips everything before the resume point.

nodes.title: Redaction-list threads
nodes.role: Two optional inputs to the merge. The from thread always runs: when the source is a redaction bookmark it lists the blocks that the earlier stream left out (so they can be sent now), otherwise it only queues an end-of-stream marker. The redact thread runs only for a redacted send and lists the blocks to leave out.

nodes.title: send_merge_thread()
nodes.role: Merges the traversal, from and redact queues in (object, block) order. A block that appears in a redaction list is turned into a REDACT range; one already redacted on both sides is dropped. Without redaction it passes the traversal's ranges through unchanged.

nodes.title: send_reader_thread()
nodes.role: Starts the read of each DATA range as soon as it is known, so the main thread rarely waits. It asks the ARC with ARC_FLAG_CACHED_ONLY and, if the block is not cached, reads it with a direct zio_read() into a private buffer, so a large send does not push other data out of the ARC. With -c it asks for compressed data (ZIO_FLAG_RAW_COMPRESS), except for metadata, embedded blocks, blocks needing a byteswap or blocks split for lack of -L; with -w it asks for the raw on-disk bytes (ZIO_FLAG_RAW). Its output queue is limited by the bytes of data in flight.

nodes.title: do_dump(): range to record
nodes.role: Runs in the ioctl thread. Picks the record for each range and, for DATA, waits for its read. A read error fails the send with EIO, unless zfs_send_corrupt_data is set, in which case the block is sent filled with the pattern 0x2f5baddb10c. A block larger than 128K without -L is cut into 128K WRITE records; an embedded block pointer with -e becomes WRITE_EMBEDDED; OBJECT_RANGE ranges are dropped unless the send is raw.

nodes.title: Object records (OBJECT, FREEOBJECTS, OBJECT_RANGE)
nodes.role: OBJECT carries the dnode's type, block size, bonus type and the bonus buffer (block size clamped to 128K without -L). A raw OBJECT also carries nlevels, maxblkid and the whole encrypted bonus area. Unallocated object numbers become FREEOBJECTS records, merged when adjacent. OBJECT_RANGE (raw only) carries the salt, IV and MAC of one block of dnodes. On a resumed send, objects before the resume object are not sent again.

nodes.title: Data records (WRITE, WRITE_EMBEDDED, SPILL)
nodes.role: WRITE carries object, offset, logical size and the block. For a compressed or raw block it also carries the compression type and compressed size, and for raw the salt, IV, MAC and byteswap flag. When a block pointer is available (not for split, embedded or decrypted blocks) the record also carries its checksum, flagged when that checksum is strong enough for dedup. WRITE_EMBEDDED carries the few bytes decoded from an embedded block pointer. SPILL carries an object's spill block; unmodified spill blocks are also sent, flagged, so old receivers do not drop them.

nodes.title: FREE and REDACT records
nodes.role: FREE tells the receiver that a byte range of an object holds no data: holes found by the traversal, and the region past the end of every object sent. Adjacent frees are merged into one pending record. Frees are sent in full streams too (DRR_FLAG_FREERECORDS), so that a full stream can be received as a clone. REDACT marks ranges left out of a redacted stream.

nodes.title: dump_record(): checksum and output
nodes.role: Adds the record header to the running fletcher-4 checksum, stores that checksum in the header (every record except BEGIN), adds the payload, and writes header and payload through the stream's output function. The checksum always covers everything before the field it is stored in, so END's checksum covers the whole stream.

nodes.title: arc_read()
nodes.role: Shared with the I/O flow graph. Serves the traversal's indirect and dnode blocks, the sender's ARC_FLAG_CACHED_ONLY lookups (a hit hands back a buffer, a miss returns an error instead of reading), the receive prefetches and the corrective receive's check read.

nodes.title: zio create + execute

ref.code: zio_rewrite(zio_t *pio, spa_t *spa, uint64_t txg, blkptr_t *bp, abd_t *data,

nodes.role: Shared with the I/O flow graph. The sender's direct reads of uncached blocks, the receiver's writes at txg sync, and the corrective receive's in-place rewrite and verification read enter the zio pipeline here.

nodes.title: Stream bytes (pipe, file, ssh)
nodes.role: Whatever carries the bytes from `zfs send` to `zfs receive`: a pipe, a file, ssh or a network tool. ZFS adds no framing beyond the records themselves, each a fixed-size dmu_replay_record_t header followed by its payload.

nodes.title: receive_resume_token
nodes.role: Read-only property of a dataset whose resumable receive was interrupted. Built on demand from the DS_FIELD_RESUME_* entries of the dataset or of its tofs/%recv child: fromguid, object, offset, bytes, toguid, toname and the -L / -e / -c / -w flags of the original stream, packed as an nvlist, gzip-compressed, checksummed with fletcher-4 and hex-encoded.

nodes.title: zfs receive (cmd/zfs)
nodes.role: Parses the receive options: -F force, -s resumable, -A abort (destroys the saved resumable state), -c heal an existing snapshot, -o / -x property overrides, -d / -e name mapping, -u no mount. Refuses to read the stream from a terminal.

nodes.title: libzfs: zfs_receive() / zfs_receive_one()
nodes.role: Reads and checks the BEGIN record (magic, byte order, stream type). A compound stream goes to the package code. A single stream goes to zfs_receive_one(), which works out the destination name and enforces the userspace rules: a full stream into an existing dataset needs -F and a dataset without snapshots, -F may not destroy an encrypted dataset, and an existing filesystem that a full stream replaces is unmounted first. Then it passes the BEGIN record and the file descriptor to libzfs_core.

nodes.title: libzfs: replication receive
nodes.role: For a compound stream: reads the list of filesystems and snapshots, renames and promotes to match the sender, and with -F destroys snapshots and filesystems that are not in the stream. Then receives each substream in turn through zfs_receive_impl().

nodes.title: libzfs_core: recv_impl()
nodes.role: Issues the receive ioctl. Resumable, healing and raw receives, and streams with a BEGIN payload, use ZFS_IOC_RECV_NEW with an nvlist (snapname, begin_record, input_fd, force, resumable, heal, properties); anything else uses the legacy ZFS_IOC_RECV. The stream itself is never copied through userspace.

nodes.title: Receive ioctl
nodes.role: Kernel entry and the order of the whole receive: dmu_recv_begin(), set received and -o / -x properties, dmu_recv_stream(), then for a mounted target suspend the filesystem (or zvol), dmu_recv_end(), and resume it on the new contents. A mounted target stays usable while the stream is applied; it is only suspended for the switch.

nodes.title: dmu_recv_begin()
nodes.role: Checks the BEGIN magic (byteswapped streams are accepted and swapped), starts the stream checksum with the BEGIN record, reads and unpacks the BEGIN payload, and runs the begin sync task: the resume variant when the stream has the RESUMING feature flag. For a full, non-raw receive it also turns -o encryption properties into crypto parameters for the new dataset.

nodes.title: dmu_recv_end()
nodes.role: Runs the end sync task, the new-dataset or the existing-dataset variant. On failure cleans up as for an interrupted stream. On success creates zvol device nodes for a new volume and its snapshot.

nodes.title: dmu_recv_cleanup_ds(): failed receive
nodes.role: Runs when the stream or the end task fails. Waits for the current txg to sync so the last saved resume state is on disk, then either keeps the inconsistent dataset (resumable receive that got past its first records) or destroys it (the new dataset or tofs/%recv). A corrective receive never destroys its snapshot.

nodes.title: dsl_sync_task()
nodes.role: The mechanism for changing the pool's dataset structure. The caller runs the check function in open context, queues the check and sync pair on the open txg and waits for that txg to sync; dsl_pool_sync() then runs the check again and the sync function in syncing context. Everything a sync function changes lands on disk in that one txg.

nodes.title: Begin check and sync
nodes.role: Decides where the stream goes. Target missing: the stream must be full or a clone stream, and the dataset is created under its final name. Target present: no tofs/%recv and no resume state may exist, the new snapshot name must be free, and for an incremental stream a snapshot with the stream's fromguid must exist; without -F the target must be unmodified since its latest snapshot, which must be that one (ETXTBSY otherwise), and with -F an older snapshot is accepted. A full stream onto an existing dataset needs -F and is refused for encrypted datasets. Raw streams need the encryption feature and no embedded data.

nodes.title: End check and sync (the switch)
nodes.role: The atomic switch, in one txg. Existing target: with -F, destroy every snapshot newer than the from snapshot; swap the contents of tofs/%recv into tofs (discarding any changes made to tofs since that snapshot); snapshot tosnap; destroy %recv. New dataset: snapshot tosnap. Either way the new snapshot gets the sender's guid (drr_toguid), so a later incremental stream finds it, and the inconsistent flags and resume entries are cleared. A corrective receive changes nothing here.

nodes.title: Receiving dataset (new or tofs/%recv)
nodes.role: The dataset the records are written into: a new dataset under its final name, the hidden clone tofs/%recv of the from snapshot when the target exists, or for -c the existing snapshot itself. It is owned by the receive and flagged DS_FLAG_INCONSISTENT, so it cannot be mounted or sent normally until the end sync task. With -s it holds the DS_FIELD_RESUME_* entries (toguid, toname, fromguid, object, offset, bytes and the stream flags) that make up the resume token.

nodes.title: Raw receive keys

ref.code: dsl_crypto_recv_raw(const char *poolname, uint64_t dsobj, uint64_t fromobj,

nodes.role: A raw stream carries the dataset's wrapped master and HMAC keys, key format and PBKDF2 parameters and the meta-dnode layout in the BEGIN nvlist (crypt_keydata). They are written as they are, never unwrapped, so the receiving system needs no key. A new dataset gets them at once in their own sync task; for an existing dataset only the objset is set up then and the key is installed in the end sync task.

nodes.title: dmu_recv_stream(): reader
nodes.role: Runs in the ioctl thread. Installs the raw keys, checks a resumed stream's start point, starts the writer thread, then reads records one by one, validates each header (recv_check_drr_*), reads its payload, prefetches the indirect blocks that WRITE records will need, and queues the record for the writer. Stops at END, on an error or on a signal, then waits for the writer. A full stream received as a clone also frees every object above the highest one the stream mentioned.

nodes.title: Record read and checksum check
nodes.role: Reads straight from the stream's file descriptor with zfs_file_read(). The running fletcher-4 checksum over everything read so far must equal the checksum in each new header (headers with a zero checksum are not checked), and END must carry the checksum of the whole stream. A mismatch fails the receive with ECKSUM; an early end of the stream gives ZFS_ERR_STREAM_TRUNCATED. Both leave resumable state behind when -s was given.

nodes.title: receive_writer_thread()
nodes.role: Takes records off the queue in stream order and hands each to its handler. Any record other than WRITE first flushes the pending batch of WRITE records. After an error it keeps draining and freeing records until the end-of-stream marker. At the end it replays any deferred records, flushes the last batch and wakes the reader.

nodes.title: save_resume_state()
nodes.role: With -s, records the object and offset of the last OBJECT, WRITE or WRITE_EMBEDDED record applied in a tx, and the stream bytes read so far, in the dataset's in-memory slot for that tx's txg. dsl_dataset_sync() writes the slot to the dataset's ZAP when the txg syncs, so the resume point on disk always matches data that is on disk. While records are deferred the point is held at the first deferred record.

nodes.title: receive_object()
nodes.role: Applies OBJECT: claims a free object number with the stream's type, block size, bonus and dnode size, or reclaims an existing object whose type, block size or bonus changed (freeing its old contents first), sets checksum and compression, copies in the bonus buffer, and for raw streams sets the dnode layout and the dnode block's encryption parameters. When an object number must be reused at a different dnode size, the old dnode's free has to sync first; instead of a txg wait per object the claim and every later record touching those slots are parked and replayed after one txg wait (not for raw or corrective receives).

nodes.title: receive_freeobjects() / receive_free()
nodes.role: FREEOBJECTS frees every allocated object in its range (skipping the inner slots of large dnodes). FREE frees a byte range of an object with dmu_free_long_range(), which works in chunks of separate transactions. REDACT is applied as a FREE.

nodes.title: WRITE batch: lightweight writes
nodes.role: Collects consecutive WRITE records of one object (they must arrive in increasing object, offset order) and applies the batch in a single tx. A record that matches the object's block size is written as a lightweight write: the record's buffer becomes the block, with no dbuf and no ARC copy, which is safe because nothing can read the dataset before the receive ends. A compressed record is written still compressed and a raw record still encrypted, with the record's salt, IV and MAC. A record of another size is decompressed if needed and written with dmu_write_by_dnode().

nodes.title: receive_write_embedded() / receive_spill()
nodes.role: WRITE_EMBEDDED puts the record's bytes back into a block pointer (or, if the record does not match the object's block size, decompresses it and writes it normally). SPILL replaces the object's spill block with a loaned ARC buffer, a raw one for raw streams; unmodified spill records are ignored by receivers that know the spill-block flag.

nodes.title: receive_object_range() (raw)
nodes.role: Raw streams only: keeps the salt, IV, MAC and byte order of one block of dnodes until the next OBJECT record in that block applies them, so the received dnode block gets the same encryption parameters as on the sender.

nodes.title: Corrective receive (zfs receive -c)
nodes.role: Uses only WRITE records, against an existing snapshot. Reads the block; only a checksum error (ECKSUM) makes it a candidate. Recompresses (and for an encrypted dataset re-encrypts with the block's own salt and IV) the record's data into the block's on-disk form, recomputes the checksum and requires it to equal the block pointer's, then rewrites the same disk locations and reads the block back; on success the block leaves the pool's error log. A block that cannot be reproduced fails the receive unless zfs_recv_best_effort_corrective is set.

nodes.title: dmu_tx (transaction)

ref.code: dmu_tx_hold_write_by_dnode(dmu_tx_t *tx, dnode_t *dn, uint64_t off, int len)

nodes.role: Shared with the I/O flow graph. Every receive handler declares what it will change and joins the open txg like any writer, so receive is subject to the same write throttle.

nodes.title: dmu_object claim / reclaim / free
nodes.role: Object allocation at a number chosen by the caller, as receive needs: claim a free number, reallocate an existing object with new properties, or free one.

nodes.title: dmu_free_long_range()
nodes.role: Frees a byte range of an object in chunks, each in its own transaction, waiting for the next txg when too many frees are dirty, so that a large free does not build one huge txg.

nodes.title: dmu_write family
nodes.role: Shared with the I/O flow graph. Receive uses three entries: the lightweight write, which turns a whole-block buffer into a dirty record directly; the ordinary write, which copies into dbufs; and the embedded write, which stores data in the block pointer.

nodes.title: dbuf_dirty() + dirty records
nodes.role: Shared with the I/O flow graph. Besides ordinary dirty records on dbufs, receive creates lightweight dirty records that hold only an abd and its write properties, and dirty records whose overridden block pointer holds embedded data.

nodes.title: dnode (object)

ref.code: dnode_hold_impl(objset_t *os, uint64_t object, int flag, int slots,
dnode_allocate(dnode_t *dn, dmu_object_type_t ot, int blocksize, int ibs,
dnode_free_range(dnode_t *dn, uint64_t off, uint64_t len, dmu_tx_t *tx)

nodes.role: Shared with the I/O flow graph. Receive allocates and reallocates dnodes at the object numbers the stream names, frees ranges, and collects the txg's dirty records under the dnode.

nodes.title: Prefetch (dmu_zfetch)

ref.code: dmu_prefetch(objset_t *os, uint64_t object, int64_t level, uint64_t offset,

nodes.role: Shared with the I/O flow graph. The receive reader issues explicit prefetches of level-1 indirect blocks for upcoming WRITE records, so the writer finds them in the ARC.

nodes.title: TXG: syncing (txg_sync_thread)
nodes.role: Shared with the I/O flow graph. Sync tasks and failed receives wait here for their txg to reach disk.

nodes.title: spa_sync()
nodes.role: Shared with the I/O flow graph. Writes one txg, including the received data and the sync tasks of receive begin and end.

nodes.title: dsl_pool_sync()
nodes.role: Shared with the I/O flow graph. Syncs the dirty datasets (writing a receiving dataset's saved resume point into its ZAP on the way), then runs the queued sync tasks of that txg.

nodes.title: dbuf_sync_leaf() / dbuf_write()
nodes.role: Shared with the I/O flow graph. A lightweight dirty record from receive becomes a write zio directly from its abd and saved properties, with no dbuf and no ARC buffer involved.

model: A send stream is a flat sequence of records that describe objects and blocks, not files: BEGIN, then OBJECT, FREEOBJECTS, OBJECT_RANGE, WRITE, WRITE_EMBEDDED, SPILL, FREE and REDACT records in (object, offset) order, then END. Every record header carries a running fletcher-4 checksum of everything before it, and END carries the checksum of the whole stream.

An incremental stream is small because of birth txgs. The traversal skips every block pointer born at or before the from point's creation txg, and the whole subtree below it, so unchanged data is never even read. Only the from point's txg and guid are needed, which is why a bookmark (which keeps no blocks) works as an incremental source.

Send is a pipeline of kernel threads joined by queues that are limited in bytes: the traversal finds candidate blocks, the merge thread applies redaction, the reader thread starts the reads early (taking a block from the ARC only if it is already cached, otherwise reading it directly without filling the ARC), and the main thread turns each range into records and writes them to the file descriptor.

The send flags only change how blocks are represented. -c sends compressed blocks as they are on disk; -w sends the encrypted on-disk bytes with their salt, IV and MAC plus the wrapped keys, so no key is needed; without -L blocks over 128K are split into 128K records; -e sends tiny embedded blocks as the bytes held in the block pointer. Receive writes compressed and raw payloads to disk as they arrive, without recompressing or re-encrypting.

Userspace only frames the stream. `zfs receive` reads the BEGIN record and hands the file descriptor to the kernel, which reads every other record itself; on the send side the kernel writes the records straight to the descriptor.

Receive writes into a dataset nobody can use yet: a new dataset, or the hidden clone tofs/%recv when the target exists, flagged inconsistent. A writer thread applies the records in ordinary DMU transactions and txg sync writes them like any other dirty data.

The switch is atomic: one sync task, in one txg, snapshots the result with the sender's guid, swaps %recv into the target (after destroying newer snapshots when -F is given) and destroys the clone. Until that txg an existing target is untouched, and for an incremental stream it stays mounted and readable throughout.
With -s the position of the last applied record is saved in every txg. After an interruption the inconsistent dataset survives, and its receive_resume_token tells `zfs send -t` where to restart.
simplifications: One send range and one record of each kind is drawn per path. Real streams interleave many OBJECT, FREEOBJECTS, WRITE and FREE records in (object, offset) order, each object's OBJECT record before its data.
Redacted sends (zfs redact, --redact, sends from redaction bookmarks) are reduced to the redaction-list node; the merge rules and the REDACT handling on receive are only described.

Spill blocks, large dnodes, byteswapped streams, zvol device nodes and the receive of a full stream as a clone are mentioned in node roles but not drawn as separate steps. DRR_WRITE_BYREF (deduplicated streams) is no longer generated, and the receiver rejects it.
Properties (-p, -o, -x, received properties), holds, saved sends (-S), dry runs and size estimates, progress reporting and zfs receive -A are left out except where a label names them.
The receive writer's deferral of reallocated dnodes (receive_defer_*) is described in receive_object's role but not drawn. The reset of user accounting after a raw receive is not drawn.

Sync tasks are shown going through txg_sync, spa_sync and dsl_pool_sync like the rest of a txg. Below dbuf_sync the write pipeline (compression, checksums, allocation, vdevs) is in the I/O graph, path txg_sync.
Corrective receive reads the block through dbuf_read(); the diagram draws that as one wire to arc_read.

page.title: ZFS Send and Receive
page.intro: This diagram follows a replication stream from end to end: how `zfs send` turns a snapshot (or the difference between two points in a dataset's history) into a flat stream of records, what those records are, why an incremental stream is small, what -c, -w, -L, -e and -t change, and how `zfs receive` applies the records to a hidden, inconsistent dataset and then switches it into place in a single transaction group.
